newsitem.title: CANADA: Manitoba fusarium in wheat not as bad as '93 - MPE.
newsitem.headline: Manitoba fusarium in wheat not as bad as '93 - MPE.

text.p: Fusarium head blight infection of Manitoba's wheat and other cereal crops is extensive but not as severe as an outbreak that occured in 1993, a Manitoba Pool Elevators quality control manager said.
"1993 was the worst for fusarium and we're not even as bad as last year but it's more widespread," MPE quality control manager Derry Sager said.
Fusarium (scab) in 1993 struck Manitoba's Red River Valley cereal crops. The infection spread northwest to the Dauphin area and the Saskatchewan border this year, Sager said.
Fusarium is brought on by prolonged rain during heading.
The fungus can produce vomitoxin which in low levels are tolerable but in higher levels can cause nausea in humans and animals.

"The heat shrivelled (the heads) up and if they use enough air in the combines they can blow it out. It's not the major problem it was a few years ago," Sager said. "I'm sure we can handle the fusarium problem. It's may be downgrading grades but not much more."
Of greater concern is ergot fungus in cereals grains.
"The biggest problem is, we're seeing a lot of ergot, it's a little more widespread than fusarium," Sager said.
Ergot occurs during the flowering stage and replaces the cereal's kernel. It is toxic to both humans and livestock.
Durum wheat is more susceptible to ergot than milling wheat.

"Where it is, it's in large amounts, we're getting some that have 50 pieces in a one-lb sample, that's quite a bit. We're seeing an awful lot in barley, a lot of malting barley is going to be rejected because of ergot," Sager said.
MPE operates the largest number of primary elevators in Manitoba at more than 110. Manitoba Agriculture estimated swathing of cereals Monday at about 50 percent completed.
